# Poison gas and its prohibition (`chemical_weapons`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by chlorine_bleach, siegecraft_mining, laws_of_war, arms_control
- Core idea: Smoke and choking fumes appear in ancient accounts of sieges. The industrial powers of the First World War produced chemical weapons on a new scale. These weapons inflicted deaths, lasting injuries and fear. Protective equipment, medical care and the burden of operating in masks became part of soldiers' experience. The Geneva Protocol of 1925 prohibited the use of chemical and bacteriological methods of warfare for its parties. The prohibition was breached, including by Italy in Ethiopia and Japan in China. The later Chemical Weapons Convention requires its parties to destroy declared stockpiles under international verification.
- Pitfalls:
  - Gas was not a war-winning weapon; it caused well under a tenth of First World War casualties and a small share of deaths
  - Assuming protective equipment eliminated casualties or spared soldiers the burden of prolonged exposure
  - The 1925 protocol banned use, not possession, and held through deterrence, not law alone
  - Overlooking chemical warfare outside Europe, including Italian use in Ethiopia and Japanese use in China
- History: greece: 429 BC – Spartans burn sulphur and pitch against Plataea (Thucydides II.77); china: c. 4th c. BC – Mozi describes pumping smoke of burning plants into besiegers' tunnels with bellows; rome: c. AD 256 – Simon James interprets archaeological remains at Dura-Europos as evidence that Sasanian miners killed Roman soldiers with toxic fumes; europe: 1899 – Hague declaration against asphyxiating shells; 22 April 1915 – German chlorine cloud at Ypres; 1917 – mustard gas; 1925 – Geneva Protocol bans use of gas and bacteriological weapons; global: 1993 – Chemical Weapons Convention opens for signature; 1997 – enters into force
- Read:
  - L. F. Haber, The Poisonous Cloud: Chemical Warfare in the First World War (1986)
  - Simon James, Stratagems, Combat, and 'Chemical Warfare' in the Siege Mines of Dura-Europos, American Journal of Archaeology 115 (2011)
  - Richard M. Price, The Chemical Weapons Taboo (1997)
